## A first scientific question

This article is for a researcher beginning with repeated measurements and
basic R data frames. It requires an installed MIRA package, knitr for tables,
and ggplot2 for one figure. No model knowledge, Quarto CLI, or external data is
needed. We will create a small study, read one result, investigate one missing
observation, and preserve the analysis.

Suppose a retina clinic records best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) at
baseline and four weeks after starting a hypothetical management strategy
for diabetic macular edema. BCVA is an ETDRS letter score: more letters mean
better measured acuity. Our descriptive question is how the study eyes'
scores change between these visits. All observations and gains below are
synthetic assumptions, not estimates of a treatment's effectiveness.

There is **one prespecified study eye per participant**. In this simulation
the right eye is eligible in every participant and is selected at baseline;
we do not select the better-responding eye after follow-up. The participant
ID therefore identifies one independent person and that person's same study
eye at each visit. Both eyes from one person would require additional
dependence to be addressed; they are not independent participants. Without
a concurrent comparator, these changes do not identify a causal treatment
effect. [DRCR Retina Network's measurement study](https://public.jaeb.org/drcrnet/stdy/149)
illustrates why visual-acuity measurement and OCT anatomy are distinct
research measurements; this tutorial is not a reproduction of that trial.

A longitudinal study measures the same people repeatedly. Measurements from
one person can be correlated. Two measurements from twelve people provide
twenty-four measurements, rather than twenty-four independent participants.
Paired changes preserve the association between each person's measurements.

## Begin with two visits and a secure identity

In **wide format**, one row represents the selected study eye of one
participant and one numeric column represents BCVA at each visit. The
participant ID is a label, not a measurement or a numeric predictor. We
simulate different underlying acuities, add visit-specific measurement
variation, and round scores to whole letters. The assumed four-letter mean
gain supplies variation for learning; it is neither a treatment recommendation
nor a validated individual response threshold.

```{r data}
library(MIRA)
set.seed(3101)
n <- 12L
usual_bcva <- rnorm(n, mean = 58, sd = 8)
study_complete <- data.frame(
  participant_id = sprintf("E%02d", seq_len(n)),
  bcva_t0 = round(usual_bcva + rnorm(n, sd = 3)),
  bcva_t1 = round(usual_bcva + 4 + rnorm(n, sd = 3))
)
knitr::kable(head(study_complete), digits = 3,
  caption = "First six participants: one study eye each, BCVA in ETDRS letters at baseline (t0) and week 4 (t1).")
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(study_complete$participant_id),
          !anyNA(study_complete$participant_id),
          all(vapply(study_complete[-1L], is.numeric, logical(1L))),
          all(as.matrix(study_complete[-1L]) > 20),
          all(as.matrix(study_complete[-1L]) < 95))
```

The checks confirm complete, unique IDs, numeric columns, and the chosen
20-to-95-letter simulation range; these range checks are not general clinical
eligibility or data-cleaning rules. They
do not check whether a real-world ID was assigned to the correct person; that
requires study records. `_t0` and `_t1` let MIRA recognize one outcome,
`bcva`, and order its visits. The suffixes encode order, not physical weeks.
MIRA automatically associates `bcva` with higher-is-better, which matches
ETDRS letters here. A logMAR-valued BCVA variable requires an explicit
lower-is-better setting, as shown in the data-preparation article. Automatic
response thresholds default to zero; no clinical responder definition is
being validated in this first analysis.

## Run once and locate the information

We request the optional plot suite because this first path includes a figure.
`analyses = "plots"` requests that suite while disabling the optional model,
correlation, outlier, and arm-comparison modules. Core summaries and paired
tests still run. `<-` retains their result in `fit` for subsequent steps.

```{r first-analysis}
fit <- mira_info_long(study_complete, id = "participant_id",
                      analyses = "plots", verbose = FALSE)
class(fit)
fit$overview[c("n_patients", "n_timepoints", "complete_profiles")]
data.frame(variable = fit$time_vars, label = unname(fit$time_labels))
stopifnot(inherits(fit, "mira_info_long"),
          fit$overview$n_patients == n,
          identical(fit$time_vars, c("bcva_t0", "bcva_t1")))
```

`fit` is a `mira_info_long` list: named components hold related information.
`overview` describes supplied profiles; `time_vars` records selected columns
in order; `descriptives` holds visit summaries; `change` holds paired
comparisons; and `plots` holds drawable figures. `$` selects a component, so
`fit$descriptives` means the visit-summary table inside `fit`. The first
selected visit becomes the baseline for trajectory summaries.

`verbose = FALSE` prevents the extensive printed report, while warnings remain
visible. A non-`NULL` `analyses` selection overrides the five individual
optional switches. `analyses = "none"` would also turn off plotting; it still
computes core paired tests and the base-R Friedman branch when applicable.
The default `analyses = NULL` instead respects the individual switches, whose
defaults are all `TRUE`. This tutorial does not fit a model.

## Read a visit mean before reading a change

The **mean** at a visit is the sum of observed BCVA letter scores divided by the
number observed at that visit. The SD describes differences among participants.
The confidence interval describes uncertainty in a population mean under
independent sampling of participants; it does not contain 95% of individual
acuity letter scores.

```{r descriptives}
knitr::kable(
  fit$descriptives[c("label", "n", "mean", "sd", "ci_lower", "ci_upper")],
  col.names = c("Visit", "N", "Mean", "SD", "Lower 95% CI", "Upper 95% CI"),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Observed BCVA (ETDRS letters): t0 is baseline and t1 is week 4."
)
observed_counts <- colSums(is.finite(as.matrix(study_complete[fit$time_vars])))
stopifnot(all(fit$descriptives$n == unname(observed_counts)),
          sum(observed_counts) == 24L,
          isTRUE(all.equal(fit$descriptives$mean,
            unname(colMeans(study_complete[fit$time_vars])))))
```

Each row's `N` is twelve. There are twelve people and twenty-four finite
measurements in total. These denominators answer different questions. Missing
follow-up can change visit-specific `N` without changing the input cohort.

The outcome name was inferred, so metric fields have base names such as `mean`.
Explicitly declaring an outcome changes those names. The
[data and detection article](frequentist-long-data-and-detection.html#make-the-analysis-plan-explicit)
explains their provenance and the map for safe extraction.

## Read one paired change, its interval, and its test

For a person observed at both visits, subtract **week 4 minus baseline**.
The average of those differences estimates mean within-person change among
paired study eyes, in ETDRS letters. Positive change means more letters read. This is
the quantity of interest, or **estimand**, for our first change question.
Select its row by source names, which remain meaningful if visits are added.

```{r change}
baseline_followup <- subset(fit$change,
                            from == "bcva_t0" & to == "bcva_t1")
stopifnot(nrow(baseline_followup) == 1L)
knitr::kable(
  baseline_followup[c("n", "mean_change", "sd_change", "ci_lower", "ci_upper")],
  col.names = c("Paired N", "Mean change", "SD change", "Lower 95% CI", "Upper 95% CI"),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Paired week-4-minus-baseline BCVA change (ETDRS letters)."
)
```

The mean change is `r sprintf("%.2f", baseline_followup$mean_change)` ETDRS letters,
with a pointwise 95% interval from
`r sprintf("%.3f", baseline_followup$ci_lower)` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", baseline_followup$ci_upper)` letters. Its uncertainty comes from
participant differences. Exact Student-t coverage requires independent, normally distributed differences.
For these rounded letter scores it is a working approximation, whose adequacy
needs particular scrutiny in a small sample. The
fixed population parameter does not have a 95% frequentist probability of
lying in this particular interval.

The paired t test asks whether a population mean difference of zero is
compatible with the data and assumptions. Its two-sided p-value is
`r format.pval(baseline_followup$paired_t_p, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)`.
It is not the probability that zero change is true and does not measure
clinical importance. A large p-value would not establish equivalence. With
two visits there is one paired-t comparison, so Holm adjustment leaves its
p-value unchanged. More visits introduce a larger comparison family.

This audit reconstructs the estimate and Student-t interval from raw
differences. Reading the table does not require deriving the formula.

```{r change-audit}
differences <- study_complete$bcva_t1 - study_complete$bcva_t0
independent_ci <- mean(differences) + c(-1, 1) *
  qt(0.975, df = length(differences) - 1L) *
  sd(differences) / sqrt(length(differences))
stopifnot(baseline_followup$n == length(differences),
  isTRUE(all.equal(baseline_followup$mean_change, mean(differences))),
  isTRUE(all.equal(unname(unlist(
    baseline_followup[c("ci_lower", "ci_upper")])), independent_ci)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(baseline_followup$paired_t_p,
                   t.test(differences, mu = 0)$p.value)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(baseline_followup$paired_t_p_adj,
                   baseline_followup$paired_t_p)))
```

The p-value check uses the same base-R testing engine as MIRA: it verifies
extraction and input orientation rather than an independent test implementation.
The mean and interval are direct raw-data calculations. This small educational
sample cannot support strong clinical conclusions.

## Change one observation and predict the denominators

Keep the same twelve people, IDs, and measurements, then remove only E01's
week-4 BCVA measurement. Before running the code, predict the two visit counts and the
number of complete pairs. No new participant or response is generated.

```{r one-missing}
study_one_missing <- study_complete
study_one_missing$bcva_t1[study_one_missing$participant_id == "E01"] <- NA_real_
fit_one_missing <- mira_info_long(study_one_missing, id = "participant_id",
                                  analyses = "none", verbose = FALSE)
paired <- is.finite(study_one_missing$bcva_t0) &
  is.finite(study_one_missing$bcva_t1)
available_mean_difference <- mean(study_one_missing$bcva_t1, na.rm = TRUE) -
  mean(study_one_missing$bcva_t0)
paired_mean_difference <- mean(study_one_missing$bcva_t1[paired] -
                               study_one_missing$bcva_t0[paired])
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Quantity = c("Baseline observations", "Week-4 observations", "Complete pairs"),
  N = c(sum(is.finite(study_one_missing$bcva_t0)),
        sum(is.finite(study_one_missing$bcva_t1)), sum(paired))
), caption = "Solution: one absent follow-up changes availability, not the input cohort.")
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Quantity = c("Difference of available visit means", "Mean of paired differences"),
  Change_ETDRS_letters = c(available_mean_difference, paired_mean_difference)
), digits = 3, caption = "Two different summaries after removing E01's follow-up.")
stopifnot(identical(fit_one_missing$descriptives$n, c(12L, 11L)),
          fit_one_missing$change$n == 11L,
          isTRUE(all.equal(fit_one_missing$change$mean_change,
                           paired_mean_difference)),
          !isTRUE(all.equal(available_mean_difference, paired_mean_difference)))
```

The solution is twelve baseline observations, eleven week-4 observations, and
eleven pairs. The available-mean subtraction uses a twelve-person baseline mean
and an eleven-person follow-up mean. Paired change uses the same eleven people
on both sides. Neither calculation recovers E01's unobserved BCVA. The reason
for missingness matters for population interpretation;
[missing data](frequentist-long-missing-data.html) develops that question.

## Add a third visit without changing the earlier study

Return to the complete study and add week 12. The existing IDs and first two
measurements are preserved. This new data configuration needs a new analysis.
The suffix orders the visit; it does not supply physical elapsed weeks.

```{r third-visit}
study_three_visits <- study_complete
set.seed(3102)
study_three_visits$bcva_t2 <- round(usual_bcva + 7 + rnorm(n, sd = 3))
fit_three_visits <- mira_info_long(study_three_visits, id = "participant_id",
                                   analyses = "none", verbose = FALSE)
knitr::kable(fit_three_visits$change[c("from", "to", "n", "mean_change")],
  digits = 3, caption = "Adding week 12 creates three paired BCVA comparisons (ETDRS letters).")
stopifnot(identical(study_three_visits[names(study_complete)], study_complete),
          nrow(fit_three_visits$change) == 3L,
          isTRUE(all.equal(fit_three_visits$change$paired_t_p_adj,
            p.adjust(fit_three_visits$change$paired_t_p, method = "holm"))))
```

There are now three paired comparisons: baseline to week 4, baseline to week
12, and week 4 to week 12. Their Holm p-values form one paired-t family; the
confidence intervals remain pointwise. Adding an exploratory visit does not
automatically redefine the prespecified primary endpoint or multiplicity plan.

## Display the first analysis and retain it

Return to `fit`, the original complete **two-visit** analysis. Its stored
`mean_ci` plot answers the visit-mean question. It uses equally spaced visit
categories and shows neither participant spread nor paired-change uncertainty.

```{r first-figure, fig.cap="BCVA means (ETDRS letters) for the original twelve complete study eyes, one per participant, at baseline (t0) and week 4 (t1). Bars show pointwise 95% Student-t confidence intervals for visit means; they do not show individual spread or uncertainty in paired change."}
stopifnot(inherits(fit$plots$mean_ci, "ggplot"))
print(fit$plots$mean_ci + ggplot2::labs(y = "BCVA (ETDRS letters)"))
```

An RDS file preserves the computed R object. Use a temporary path here; use a
managed project directory for an actual study and retain its input data,
script, seed, and software versions alongside the result.

```{r save}
result_file <- tempfile("mira-bcva-", fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(fit, result_file)
restored <- readRDS(result_file)
stopifnot(identical(restored$descriptives, fit$descriptives),
          identical(restored$change, fit$change))
packageVersion("MIRA")
```

## Create a first reproducible report archive

Reuse the result just read; reporting does not refit it. This minimal call
writes a **source-only bundle**, selecting HTML as a future target. It needs
neither Quarto CLI nor TeX and opens no document.

```{r first-bundle}
bundle <- mira_report_freq_long(
  x = fit,
  output_dir = tempfile("mira-report-"),
  format = "html",
  render = FALSE,
  open = FALSE
)
data.frame(Artifact = c("Quarto source", "Runtime", "Payload", "CSV manifest"),
  Present = file.exists(c(bundle$source, bundle$runtime, bundle$payload,
                          bundle$results_manifest)))
bundle$rendered
stopifnot(all(file.exists(c(bundle$source, bundle$runtime, bundle$payload,
                            bundle$results_manifest))),
          !any(bundle$rendered),
          identical(readRDS(bundle$payload)$result$change, fit$change))
```

The QMD is report source, the runtime supplies its helpers, the payload
preserves the analysis, and the manifest locates exported CSV tables. Keep
them together, with one directory per independent bundle. No rendered HTML
has been produced: `rendered` records that status, whereas `expected_files`
only names possible targets. The payload can contain source measurements and
participant IDs; inspect the complete bundle before sharing. CSV files are
portable tables and do not preserve every R class or attribute.

The [reporting article](frequentist-long-reporting.html) develops manifest
lookup, metadata, display controls, regeneration, and optional rendering.
Temporary tutorial paths disappear eventually; bundle creation alone is not
a long-term retention strategy.

## Continue through the collection

The essential path has covered wide data, identity, one result, a changing
denominator, a figure, and an archive. Next use
[data preparation and detection](frequentist-long-data-and-detection.html) to
make configuration explicit, then
[descriptive analysis](frequentist-long-descriptive-analysis.html) to distinguish
distributions, changes, variability, and association. The
[handbook index](MIRA.html#a-learning-sequence) maps the applied and advanced
routes, including a [first model](frequentist-long-first-model.html) before the
advanced reference. The help pages `?mira_info_long` and
`?mira_report_freq_long` give the full argument contracts.
